utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we have the case called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, may it please Your Honours. Good morning. My name is Andrew Cayley. I appear with my colleague this morning, with Anna Richterova, case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cayley and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Marela Jevtovic and Milan Trbojevic on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau. And with Fabien Masson, I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. And good morning to you. So the witness is here. I assume there are no preliminaries. I see no one standing. We can proceed. Mr. Ackerman, the witness is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, before you do that, sir, may I just ask you once more - hopefully the last time - to stand up and repeat your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Karabeg. You may sit down. And as you see, we are going to proceed and hopefully conclude today with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we stopped yesterday, I asked the witness be shown Exhibit P69. And I need that to be put in front of him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have in front of you, sir, is an agreement on the formation of a community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities dated 29 April 1991. That would be about a month after the time that you attended that meeting in Banja Luka of representatives of several municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so at the end of April of 1991, 20 municipalities combined to form this community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this for the first time, and I hear it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what are you telling me, that you don't know whether or not this is a legitimate document or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that. I'm not talking about the document. I'm talking about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know that there was a community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities in existence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that Sanski Most was part of a community of municipalities, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of a community of municipalities until the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 6th of April of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at that list of municipalities, the 20 that are listed, several of those were municipalities that had a majority of Muslims, Bosniaks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None of those --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Sanski Most? There were several -- of those 20 municipalities, you're saying none of them had a majority Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to talk about this document. This is a document issued by illegal bodies. This is a document whereby Bosnia and Herzegovina was broken up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what this is. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll accept that. You told us -- you told us about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you proceed, Mr. Ackerman, because this document is dated 29th April 1991 and not 29th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps the witness can explain to the Chamber on what basis he is suggesting or affirming that this document was drawn up by illegal sources and that in his opinion it signifies the breaking down of the municipality or whatever. Because we're talking of 24th April 1991. What's your explanation, Mr. Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this document, which I see for the first time, which was allegedly signed on the 29th of April, 1991. And on the 6th of April, 1992 we disbanded the assembly, the legislative body of the municipality, which was demanding this, for Sanski Most to join this, envisaged by this agreement, that is, the community of municipalities of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Sorry, Mr. Ackerman, for having interrupted you like that. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not a problem, Your Honour. I just want to check something. I was just looking at the source of the document, Your Honour. According to the Prosecutor's records, it was given to an OTP staff member by the former secretary of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, Mr. Branko Cvijic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were talking yesterday about Mr. Vrkes mentioning a couple of names to you: Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Krajisnik, when he talked about the pressure being put on him from Banja Luka for Sanski Most to join the Banja Luka region. You, of course, have no idea whether Mr. Vrkes was telling you the truth or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me see. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He may have just done that as an excuse for what he was planning to do regarding joining Sanski Most with that association; in other words, blaming it on someone else besides himself. That's a possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. It's possible. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm conveying to you what he said. I didn't say that I personally spoke to that gentleman but that he said that they were exposed to pressure. So it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I need to have the Prosecutor give you back your statement of 24/25 July so that you can refer to it again. And sir, I'm going to refer to the same page we were looking at yesterday. And it's, I think, the second page. And you will find a paragraph that begins with the words "After that, there was a recess, because no agreement could be reached." It's page 3. It's the - one, two, three, four - fifth full paragraph on the page. Tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph, you said, "Some Serbs told me that Rasula personally went to villages in the municipality and asked people to sell their cows and buy rifles." That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why would people sell their cows and buy rifles if all they had to do was leave their light on and weapons would magically appear for free on their doorstep? It doesn't make any sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice in the beginning of 1991 that all of a sudden there were a huge excess of cows for sale?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask Rasula that; not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were there. Did you notice that there were a lot of cows for sale?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the cattle market, and I -- that was not my concern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, we have cattle markets which are usually outside town, and I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that at the checkpoints that were set up in Sanski Most, they originally were stopping everyone and then all of a sudden they just started stopping non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they issue some kind of identification stickers to Serbs to put on their cars so that the people manning the checkpoints would be able to tell Serbs from non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, that was not necessary, because Sanski Most is not a city with hundreds of thousands of inhabitants but a town with 17.000 inhabitants, so that most people knew one another. So that was not necessary. And I assume if it had been necessary, they certainly would have done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you telling the Chamber that the people manning the checkpoints were residents of Sanski Most who knew everybody?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly from Sanski Most municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 22 of the English version of your statement -- I'm sorry. It's the next page. It's page 23 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that page here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bear with us, sir. We'll find it. It's probably the fifth page. You should see a paragraph starting with the words "This was a pleasant meeting and it was arranged they would meet again at 2200 hours." It's on page 6, sir, the last full paragraph. It begins with "This was a pleasant meeting." Page number 6, last full paragraph. "This was a pleasant meeting and it was arranged they would meet again"; did you find that? I'm interested again in the last sentence of the paragraph. Referring to Rasula, you said: "He was the liaison between Sanski Most and Banja Luka and he was the point around which everything turned"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about this meeting that you went to in Banja Luka in March of 1991, and you told us that this person who was the liaison between Sanski Most and Banja Luka, the point around which everything turned, didn't go to that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that a time when the -- after the first multi-party elections, when the three major parties were operating under an agreement of cooperation and that the relationships between them were very good at that point? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you went to that meeting because Rasula was not available and you basically went as the number two person from Sanski Most. That's what you told us yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a couple of days before that, you told us that it was a meeting for presidents of assemblies and presidents of executive committees, both. Now, which one of those statements do you want to tell this Chamber is the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That question is not at all clear to me. Which statements are we referring to? Whether it was a meeting for presidents of assemblies or whether it was a meeting for presidents of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Executive committees. In fact, I think the witness has already explained that, how the president of the assembly was absent at the time, was not in town and the invitation was left on his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The problem is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman can --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When questions where asked like this and you look at the transcript later, often Mr. Ackerman gets answers to questions in a certain way that don't actually represent the reality of the situation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Cayley. Perhaps, I'm sure that Mr. Ackerman will rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first day that you testified here, sir, the 27th of May - and I'm not sure -- I've neglected to write down the transcript reference - but you told us with regard to that meeting in Banja Luka that it was a meeting of both the presidents of assemblies and the presidents of the executive committees of 17 municipalities in Krajina area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then yesterday you told us that you went there simply because Rasula, who was the invited person, couldn't go. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if you wish, I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you just did. What I'd like you to do now is look at -- I'd like you to take a look at Exhibit 602. Now, Prosecution Exhibit 602 is a document that was signed by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's a document that refers to what you've described as a violent and illegal effort to seize power in the takeover of the Sanski Most branch of the SDK on 28 February 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your testimony on May 27th, at page 46 of the LiveNote, you spoke about -- your answer was: "On the 28th of February, in the SDK there was 'a forcible takeover of power by the SDS' and that by force they wanted to replace Mrs. Dobrija," I think, "Sanica"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. After the multi-party elections were held, there was an agreement between the parties over who would get what positions in the municipality of Sanski Most, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And part of that agreement was that the -- the head of the SDK would be a Serb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that this woman who was the head of the SDK was supposed to be replaced by a Serb and refused to vacate her position? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refused? To whom? To whom did she express her refusal to leave her working post, to a gang that wanted by force to take over the SDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Before that, didn't she refuse to vacate the position in favour of the Serb person who was supposed to get that position in accordance with the agreement that had been entered into? You can answer that yes or no. Did she do that or didn't she?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman -- Mr. Ackerman, you already put the question to him whether there was an agreement -- One moment, sir. -- Whether there was an agreement, as you're suggesting, that the head of the SDK would be a Serb, and he said no. So if he said no, you have no right to put the next question that you are putting, namely that my question is before that: "Did she refuse to vacate the position in favour of the Serb person who was supposed to get that position in accordance with the agreement that had been entered into?" Because he has refused your suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I was just afraid, Your Honour, if I didn't also put the second part, that I'd be accused of violating Rule 90(H) again, and I don't want to be accused of that. I'm trying to comply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not be accused of that. But you either drop the question or you rephrase it in some other manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's dropped, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you know Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where? Well, I know him from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you known him for a significant amount of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, he took a statement from you both on 13 September 1995 and 2 August 1995, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that I gave more than one statement. I said that already yesterday. And not only a statement to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about two statements, one dated 2 August 1995, another dated 13 September 1995, that you gave to Mr. Ibric. Are you family with those two statements?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say -- you were mentioning some specific dates, and I don't remember these dates, and I gave more than one. I gave several statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... referring to the 2nd August 1995 and the 13th September 1995. He's actually seen the main one, the one of September 1995 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I was just doing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And we'll cut it short, because otherwise it goes on and on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The statement of the 2nd of August is a single-page statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is the statement of the 13th of September of 1995, which is the longer statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you now have before you the two statements I was speaking about. And they're dated, and they have what I believe to be your signature at the end of each of them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave these statements to Mr. Ibric in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never in Banja Luka. And I was never in Banja Luka with Mr. Ibric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, doesn't it say at the top of each of those documents that they are from the security services centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But with a temporary headquarters in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where it says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, look at it and see if you can find anything in the statement where it says anything about Travnik. Do you see that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Ibric an authorised official of the Banja Luka security services centre in September -- August and September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a temporary headquarters in Travnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did -- did Mr. Zupljanin, the head of Banja Luka CSB, set up a temporary headquarters in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, the interpreters have had a problem in understanding what you answered, what you replied to Mr. Ackerman's question. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll laugh at the question which was posed by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think I can understand why, because we're talking of 1995, Mr. Ackerman. So asking him about Zupljanin moving -- the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was just something that a few of you guys sitting around Travnik cooked up, that you'd have a -- a Banja Luka security services centre office in Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really seriously object. This is a court of law. It's not a circus. Mr. Ackerman knows exactly why this document says what it says. The country was split. There were dual authorities. He knows the answers to his questions. I really object in the strongest possible terms to this kind of facetious cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a very misleading document. In fact, I recall yesterday Your Honour being misled by it, because you talked about a statement that this man gave in Banja Luka, because it misled you yesterday. I just want it clear that this man was not an official of the Banja Luka security services centre in September of 1995, as he claims in these documents to be. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But Mr. Ackerman, you have had -- you put that question to the witness, and he has answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm through with it. I'm through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's told you that as far as the -- the centre -- temporary centre in Travnik is concerned, yes, Mr. Ibric was an authorised representative of the Banja Luka CS -- anyway, you know what I mean. The Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 of the statement that you made on 13 September 1995, you speak of a meeting at the cafe of Tomo Delic that you attended. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you say in that statement is that at that meeting, the SDS members told you that -- that you, meaning your police and so forth -- had to leave the SO building because they said they could not control their extremists who wanted to attack the building. And --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you said: "Then we told them that we were ready to defend ourselves in case of attack"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that building, you and your people were armed and prepared to defend yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a demand was made, was it not, that you exit the building to the front and lay down your weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was requested by the paralegal -- the illegal organs of the municipality. I would like you, Mr. Ackerman, to clearly state by who and -- who, what, and where; otherwise, I will not be answering such questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you do remember a time when you were asked to exit the building and lay down your arms, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But let me add, that was the Serb policy. Tomo Delic was asking. I cannot control the extremists. While Tomo Delic on the other hand was leading these extremist Serb forces. And throughout the time, that was the Serb policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We all understand that's your position. That's not what I was asking you, but we understand that's your position. You've told us that it's correct that you were asked to come out of the building and surrender your arms. You didn't do that. You and the other people in the building left the building with your arms, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. No, not that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But later you did. You left the building with your arms. You didn't --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Come out and lay down your arms. And some of those people went to Sehovci and some went to Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On May 28th, at page 37 of the LiveNote transcript, you were asked about whether there was any resistance in Mahala when Mahala burned; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, you were in jail.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked by the Prosecutor -- you answered "There was no resistance with regard to Mahala." And then the Prosecutor asked you, "Who did you hear that from?" And your answer was, "I heard it from Tomo Delic himself, among others." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that convinced you because of what Tomo Delic said, that there was no resistance in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what convinced you, because Tomo Delic had told you that there was no fighting in Mahala. That's how you became convinced that there was none. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- he didn't have to convince me there is nothing that I have to leave and be convinced about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at some documents. And we'll just kind of go through them in order. 603, 613, 647, 697, 718.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have an English translation of P603, and so somehow I guess we'll just have to read it, unless the -- unless there's one around somewhere. Yes. I'd appreciate that very much. Mr. Usher, Mr. Cayley has an English translation for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How come? Did you turn the page and see whether it's on the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. I just have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the one I have is a one-page document with the English version on one side and the B/C/S, Serbo-Croat version on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, my guess, Your Honour, is that when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's no problem. I just wanted to make sure that -- yes. Does the witness have -- yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the document -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, of 7 March 1992 from a person who uses the name Milos. And you can see the document. It talks about a meeting of 500 armed Muslim citizens in the village of Donji Kamengrad. It talks about Green Beret troops in the vicinity of Sanski Most. It talks about launching an armed attack on the village of Suhace. It talks about 3.000 Muslims owning long barrels, part of the SDA. And it names you as one of those responsible for the activities of the SDA in this regard. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will laugh again. You can find as many Miloses as you want who will submit to you such documents. And I'm surprised you don't have more of such documents with such a signature with Milos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, you answer the question and just the question. And please don't enter into arguments with the Defence counsel. The Defence counsel is doing his duty here, and he has a right to put the question to you. And you just answer yes, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you provoke him, he will provoke you, and then I will have to intervene. And when I intervene, one of you or both of you will suffer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this document is designated P603. That means it's a Prosecutor's exhibit. Do you know that? Do you know that? Apparently the witness has decided to stop answering questions, Your Honour, or he's not hearing my questions or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. And I just said this, what is concluded here, that Milos found and concluded this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg the question is a very simple one: Do you know, are you aware that this document which is numbered P603 has not been brought forward by the Defence but has been brought forward by the Prosecutor? This is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's it. Finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at Exhibit P613, please. P613, sir, is another Prosecutor's Exhibit. It's dated 14 April 1992. And I want to refer you to the last paragraph. It's a document from the Banja Luka security services centre. The last paragraph says: "The most recent incident of a mass gathering of armed Serbian and Muslim inhabitants in Sanski Most, caused by explosives being placed on a building belonging to a Serb, led to demands for the territory of the municipality to be divided." Do you recall that mass gathering of armed Serbian and Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The date, approximately we're talking of prior to the 14th April 1992 but very near that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall such a gathering?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you, sir, please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the last paragraph of the document, beginning with "The most recent incident"?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say, there were the joint guards of citizens of Muslim and Serb and Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Do you recall an incident involving a mass gathering of armed Serbian and Muslim inhabitants because of a bomb that was placed on Serb property?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The problem -- the problem is, if you look at the original version, the very last paragraph is actually what the witness is reading. It's -- it's an understandable mistake. In the English version, it's one single last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, it's essentially two split paragraphs. So the witness is reading the wrong paragraph, and that's why there's this miscommunication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Cayley for bringing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, look at the paragraph beginning with the word [B/C/S spoken]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do see it. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the paragraph I'm referring to. And all I want to know from you is do you recall such an incident sometime prior to 14 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: An explosion -- an -- two grenades were launched against the mosque in Donji Kamengrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, look at me. We are not talking of the launching of two grenades in the courtyard of the mosque. We're talking of an incident occurring prior -- approximate to the 14th April 1992 where an explosion did take place but not in the mosque but an explosion took place on a building belonging to a Serb. We're not talking of a mosque here. As a result of this explosion taking place on a building belonging to a Serb, it is being alleged that there was then a mass gathering - not a small gathering but a mass gathering - of armed Serbian and Muslim inhabitants of Sanski Most. The question is this: Do you remember an explosion taking place on a building of a Serb before but approximate to the date of the 14th April 1992? Question number one. Question number two: Is the statement here that following that explosion, there was a mass gathering of armed Serbian and Muslim inhabitants of Sanski Most a correct one or is it not correct? Do you recall these two events, which are connected? That's the question that Mr. Ackerman put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That could only be when -- when this hand grenade was launched on the courtyard of a facility which was owned by a Serb. That was the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look now, sir, at P647. This is another document from this person Milos. It's again a Prosecutor's exhibit. I only want to refer you to the first part of it. It says: "In the area of Sanski Most and Kljuc, there are still ongoing battles against extremist members of the state security service who are resisting the legal authorities and do not wish to return weapons they received from the SDB or BH Territorial Defence. In the last two to three days in the Sanski Most area, a member of our forces has been killed and a few wounded, while seven SDA extremists have been killed and 64 captured or arrested." Now, the date of this, sir, is 29 May. Do you know anything about the incidents that are described in that document? And if you don't, just say you don't.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these events. As I have already said, I was imprisoned and I couldn't witness it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 697, sir. This is another document -- this is a document from the Sanski Most public security station. It talks -- and it's dated 2 July 1992. It speaks of the combat operations that took place on the territory of Sanski Most and the disarming of paramilitary formations, extremists of Muslim and Croatian nationality. And then at the bottom, you see a list of the weapons that were either handed in or confiscated during these events. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among those weapons, there are automatic rifles, 278; 11 light machine-guns; 6 zoljas, rocket launchers; 8 hand grenades; 13 mines; 3.140 kilogrammes of explosives; and 5.000 rounds of ammunition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this is correct or not. It could have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final document I want you to look at then, sir, in this series is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told that his answer was not -- I'm told that he said "There could have been arms," as opposed to "It could have been" -- "there were arms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, again, there seems to be a problem with the interpretation. When Mr. Ackerman put to you the last question about the gathering, surrendering, and confiscation of all those weapons, what did you answer? What was your answer? Did you say "Well, I don't know whether this is correct or not. It could have been"? Or did you answer also that there could have been arms or weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "Yes. I don't know whether there could have been -- there could have been arms and weapons at Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. The people did not surrender their arms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Mr. Ackerman? Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 718, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's still the case that the answer he gave was not properly translated initially. And I would ask that the tape of his answer be consulted and a proper transcript made of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please make note of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P718, sir, is a -- basically a follow-up of the previous document regarding the confiscation of weapons. And it just says: "Since our last report, we have confiscated a few additional weapons: 3 automatic rifles, 3 pistols, 200 kilogrammes of explosives" that's what it says; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can Mr. Ackerman actually read out the rest of this document, the last line, please. So we get a complete picture of what the document's actually saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says that these were weapons that were buried in the ground that had become rusty and were now useless. And that's what that says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you expect me to answer that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only expect you to confirm that what the exhibit says is what I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your question once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P718, sir, is basically a follow-up of the previous document regarding the confiscation of weapons. And it just says: "Since our last report, we have confiscated a few additional weapons: 3 automatic rifle, 3 pistols, 200 kilogrammes of explosives." Then the final paragraph refers to weapons that were buried in the ground, had rusted, and become useless. That's what the document says, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what the document says, that you read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You were arrested, you've told us, sir, on 25 May and placed in a cell of the prison near the Sanski Most police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were two cells there, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were placed in a cell right next to that which was occupied by Adil Draganovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Chamber the cell that you were in.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. I think it was a cell of some 3 by 2 metres, 3 metres by 2, which had a window with bars, but the window was edged in sheet steel, and there were small holes drilled in that steel so that a little air could come through. So the window was covered with this sheet of steel with little holes in it. On the right-hand side, there was a bed. On the left-hand side, another bed. So that between those two beds, there was some 20 centimetres of space. There was an iron door with a small opening, which was always closed, which they opened only when the guards entered to speak to us. In that cell, we also had a mattress. I don't know whether I managed to describe it well for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour were the walls of the cell? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. They were probably white. I assume they were white. I believe they were white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the walls change colour during the time you were in there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me see. I didn't pay attention to the walls, because there was no light and when we were there it was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was humidity, so probably due to the humidity they did. But really, don't ask me that. I didn't pay attention to such details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the cell that was occupied by Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us a few moments ago that Tomo Delic had made it clear when he came to see you at the jail that there was no resistance in Mahala. I'd like you now, sir, to look at that statement you gave to -- the 13 September 1995 statement to Zijad Ibric. And I think you have it there on the left. And on the English version, the part I'm referring to is at page 4. Since it doesn't have paragraphs, it's very difficult. But I think maybe it's marked -- no, it's not. It speaks -- it's the fourth page of the English version, probably maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Line 17 I think is what you're after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It talks about the 27th of May 1992 when Tomo Delic and Nemanja Tripkovic came to the jail to see you. Right? Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I'm looking for the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on page 3. And if you'd just look up a little ways from the bottom, you'll see the names "Tomo Delic" and "Nemanja Tripkovic" on page 3. It's about ten lines or so up from the bottom. Do you see the names on page 3? There's a "3" at the top of the page. Look at the top of the page and look for the number "3."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have number 3. I have 4 -- 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just go up from the bottom, you'll see the names Tomo Delic --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you said in that statement was "At that time Tomo Delic told us that Mahala had allegedly put up resistance," which was not true. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: I said that Tomo Delic said that he had a videotape of the burning of Mahala, of Mahala in flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us in your testimony, sir, on the 28th of May at page 37, you told this Trial Chamber that you knew there was no resistance. You said in answer to a question from Mr. Cayley regarding Mahala: "Answer: There was no resistance." "Question: Who did you hear that from?" "Answer: I heard it from Tomo Delic, among others." Now, that was your answer. In your statement you say: "Tomo Delic told us that Mahala had allegedly put up resistance." Now, those are not the same thing, are they?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Tomo Delic was in Mahala, that he took us out that evening to see the smoke from Mahala burning, and Tomo Delic said that he had a videotape of this burning of Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a woman sitting over there in front of a computer. What she does is write down -- she writes down every word you say, and then I get what she writes down printed like this, your exact words.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I say you said in the transcript a certain thing, that's because she wrote it down when you said it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm quite sure that that is what I did say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I recall the witness repeating the same statement this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were asked about explosions in Sanski Most of buildings. And Mr. Cayley asked you if there were any Serb buildings that suffered explosions. And you said you knew of one. I think that you called the Pilot or something like that, maybe a cafe. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Madeira in Zdenac owned by Marko Rajlic? Wasn't that blown up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Kagian Kafic [phoen], owned by a fellow named Lukic? Wasn't that blown up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, in all fairness, keeping in mind that according to the witness he was imprisoned on the 25th of May, are we talking of events prior or post the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think prior, Your Honour, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think we need to know this. Because it -- I wouldn't consider it that fair asking the question to the witness if you're referring to events that took place after the 25th of May, of which he may not be aware. I mean, he may be replying to your questions on the assumption that these events took place before his arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to look at document DB84 A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no -- it's only in English. And could you put it on the ELMO, please, because I somehow have misplaced my copy of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this appears to be a document -- and it's difficult for me to tell. The Prosecutor may know more about it than I do. But it appears that it was authored by some members of a humanitarian organisation of some form that visited Sanski Most in early 1992. It speaks of a meeting that a team came from Sarajevo and had a meeting with Rasula, Karabeg, it looks like Pranic and Majkic. Do you recall such a meeting where the four of you met with some representatives from Sarajevo of a Red Cross organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm making a supposition here, but I think -- I think that this document is ECMM, because it's referring to RC Sarajevo. I don't think that's Red Cross. I think it's regional centre Sarajevo. I also make that assumption upon the basis that it's signed by two individuals, one Terp, a Dane, the other a Spaniard, both countries that were members of the European Community. So that's my belief. Also the format of the report is such. But I will find out exactly. But that, I think, is what this document purports to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I very much appreciate Mr. Cayley's assistance, because I have no idea where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps now you could rephrase your question, making it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- because you did specify the Red Cross. It's being suggested now, and I think the suggestion is more realistic one than the Red Cross supposition -- that there could have been a meeting between representatives of the European Community and the four gentlemen that were mentioned before, that is, Rasula Nedeljko, Karabeg Mirzet, Pranic Ivica, and Majkic Dragan, are near or on the 24th of February 1992. And the first question to you, Mr. Karabeg: Do you recall meeting with some representatives of the European Community together with the other four -- three persons that I mentioned round about or on the 24th of February of 1992 in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several meetings with representatives of the European Community. To be quite frank with you, I don't really remember. But it's quite possible that this meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, he's back in your hands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the document indicates -- and I know it's not in your language, so I will just read it and it will be translated for you. It says that there are over 5.000 unemployed in Sanski Most. Why is it that there would have been 5.000 people unemployed in early 1992, before 24 February?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no work. Even now there are more than 5.000 unemployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- thank you. The next paragraph, sir, reads as follows: "All the complains --" and that means complaints, I assume -- "remarked in the last visit, 24 October, have been solved. Only problem is that since November around 20 explosions have targeted citizens' properties in the town - cafes, bars, cars ...- however they are not focussed on one exclusive nationality but in all three of them." That's what the report says. And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what the report says, that is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm not asking you if that's what the report says. I'm asking you if that statement in the report is correct, that the explosions between November and the date of this report were not focussed on one exclusive nationality but in all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know a gentleman by the name of Hase Osmancevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and he enter any kind of a joint effort to accumulate some funds and purchase weapons for members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Idriz Karabeg is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your brother?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the one. There may be several Idrez Karabeg's. But the father's name is important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a brother by that name who is a lawyer in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he stayed in Sanski Most throughout the war, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was never arrested, was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know if your own brother was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the period I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then please be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to that period, from the time you left till the time you returned.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then put it like that. I would like to ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just did. Now answer it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your brother arrested between the time you left Sanski Most and the time you returned, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 19, line 5, the transcript indicates - and I think it was just a misunderstanding of what you said. The transcript indicates that you said you were evicted to the court in Zenica. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says that you answered a question and part of your answer was that you were evicted to the court in Zenica. I don't think that's what you said, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I think if you have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't make things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Karabeg. I suggest to you to go to the page -- relative page and read out to the witness what the question was and what his answer was. In other words, we want to establish first and foremost the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's -- I don't think it's important enough to take up the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second day of your testimony, on page 23 of the transcript you were asked by Mr. Cayley about Colonel Anicic, and Mr. Cayley asked, "Do you know what his function was at this time within Sanski Most?" And your answer was: "Well, you see at the time -- and in those contacts, I had no contact with him. But as far as I was informed and as far as we knew, he headed the Crisis Staff of the municipality of -- that is, the Serbian municipality of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a slip of the tongue there. The Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just wanted to make sure that we got that cleared up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. I made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... P626, please, sir. Now, on the first day of your testimony here, Mr. Cayley was asking you about signatures and stamps and how you can tell if documents are authentic. I want you to look at this document and tell me if you see anything that would cause you to believe that this is an authentic document, since it has neither signature nor stamp.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's see. Probably, since there's a number to it and a date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think if it has a number and a date that that indicates to you that it's authentic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it purports to be a document from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- to your knowledge, the Crisis Staff didn't have an Air Force, did it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, there were no anti-aircraft weapons in Sanski Most in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this conclusion from the Crisis Staff, if you'll look about two thirds through, bans flights over the territory of Sanski Most municipality except by aircraft of the Yugoslav People's Army, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read it through. "The flight of all aircrafts not bearing the symbols of the Yugoslav People's Army --" yes, one that is not announced in advance. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally I want you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The same document or another document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same document or another document, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The same one. 694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll leave it till after the break, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will finish in 30 seconds, my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we'll go to 694. That's the first piece of good news we've heard for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't realise I was that bad this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have the document in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you notice that --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision you mean. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's called a decision. Now, you notice this one has no signature, no stamp, no number, no date. And so by your rules for what is a valid document, this document is not authentic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have the essential elements. It has been written, but it doesn't have the essential elements for it to be said to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And most probably what this is, is a draft that was never issued, never signed, never issued, isn't it? Isn't that the most likely case?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Karabeg, before I can tell you whether your labours are over or not, I'd like to know from Mr. Cayley whether there is a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, but very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very little. And then we have to decide whether there are any questions from our side. So we will now have a 30-minute break, after which, Mr. Karabeg, you will be escorted back to this courtroom. It won't be long this time and you will be on your way back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to everyone. It's my fault we are starting a little bit later than the 30 minutes allocated before. The reason is I had a very urgent call that I had to attend to, so -- Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I should simply like to present the excuses of Mr. Fabien Masson, who will be absent from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any news about the new arrival?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zecevic will arrive in The Hague today. I believe that the decision -- official decision has still not been made regarding his designation, but he will be present in The Hague this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to attend a meeting that has been scheduled for 1.00 today, if it's not been changed, here in the Tribunal. And so I may be absent during the last session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And who will take over?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Mr. Cayley. Sir, Mr. Karabeg, look at me. You're going to be asked very few questions again by Mr. Cayley, and that will bring us to an end. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I will be very brief with you. You've been testifying a long time. But I have a few matters to clarify with you. I want you to direct your mind to the 20th of April of 1992, to the meeting that you attended in Sanski Most with General Talic, the accused in this case. And I want to remind you of a question that you were asked yesterday and the response that you gave to that particular question. And the question was put to you by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic. And this is page 50 of the draft transcript, as follows. And she was referring Prosecutor's Exhibit 759, Rasula's diary, which I'm not going to put in front of you. It's not necessary for the purposes of my question. But she was directing to you to the bottom of the page. And she said the followings. "At the very bottom of this page, you find the name that was pronounced by General Talic. Kupres, Bosanski Brod, and Vukovar. You said yesterday that certain Muslims took this to be a threat. Is that right?" And your answer was: "Yes, and I was one of them." Do you recall that evidence from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it was put to you about certain events that happened in Croats where it was stated that members of the Serb population had been massacred by Croats in Kupres and that, I think, the Serb population had been massacred and expelled in the municipality of Bosanski Brod. Now, the third place that was mentioned was Vukovar. Do you recall Vukovar being mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if Your Honours could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 802, which is a public document but I've provided copies to the Defence. I can provide copies to the Defence now and to Your Honours. It is an extract of a book called "Origins of catastrophe," by Warren Zimmerman who was the last United States ambassador to what was then Yugoslavia. And on page 156 of that book, he describes as the United States ambassador the events in Vukovar in the late summer and early autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately, Mr. Karabeg, the document is in English. But I will read part of it to you and if you could listen carefully. And it is the final paragraph on page 156. And it reads as follows: --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If a copy of it could be placed on the ELMO, that will actually assist the interpreters. Could you move it down -- up. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "During the late summer and early autumn of 1991, the JNA made a fateful transition from securing territory for Serbs to targeting civilian populations. It began to shell two Croatian cities, Vukovar and Dubrovnik. The pretty Croatian city of Vukovar, with a mixed population, of which a third was Serbian, came under JNA shelling in August, apparently because of its strategic location on the Danube River between Serbia and Croatia. For three months the army, shrinking from a direct attack that might have cost it casualties, surrounded the city and shelled it to pieces. The civilian population of the city -- Serbs and Croats alike -- huddled in cellars." "A month into the siege, I asked Kadijevic and Your Honours" -- I don't think it will be disputed Kadijevic was the Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia at the time -- "what the JNA's military objective was in Vukovar; he brushed off the question as if it weren't worthy of his attention. Hundreds of civilians were killed in the shelling before the JNA finally 'liberated' the city." And then it goes on to talk about events in the Vukovar hospital, which I won't read out. Mr. Karabeg, on April the 20th, 1992, when you were in this meeting with General Talic were you aware of events that had taken place in the summer of 1991 in the city of Vukovar in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Via the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your evidence, both in chief and in cross-examination, that you took the mention of those three locations as a threat. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the reason that you took the mention of Vukovar as a threat because of what I have just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, Vukovar. Because only for Vukovar we knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the attack on Sanski Most commence? What was the date? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack commenced on Sanski Most -- commenced on the 26th of May at 9.00 p.m. It was the evening of the 26th of May to the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, you were in a prison cell at 9.00 p.m. on the 26th of May. But what did you hear that night from your prison cell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Karabeg. I think he's answered -- the previous question he's answered already. And this question he had answered already, and it was to a question that you put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to make a linkage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is a re-examination. I know what you are after. Please try to restrict --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's important, Your Honour. I'll do it very briefly. But I want to make a linkage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Karabeg, what you heard at 9.00 p.m. on the 26th of May, 1992, in your prison cell in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the evening I heard the shelling of Sanski Most. And in close proximity a grenade launcher -- a mortar launcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move straight on. Now, you were asked a number of questions if you recall about the Islamic declaration by Alija Izetbegovic. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were read various captured sentences from that book, which I'm not going to repeat to you. But you will recall that it was put to you that the SDA political policy was to create an independent Muslim state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And your reply was "never." Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever read the Islamic declaration?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina is not even mentioned in that book? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that that book was written in 1970, 22 years before the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina that this trial is concerned with? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, regarding SDA policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina and you being president of the executive committee of Sanski Most, I think you will have been familiar with that policy. I want you to state this very briefly, but can you tell the Judges, as far as you understood, what SDA policy was in 1992 towards the other ethnic groups that lived in Bosnia at the time, specifically the Croats and the Serbs. What was SDA policy as far as you understood?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Bosnia and Herzegovina united and unified in -- within its territories, co-existance of the three constituent nations, Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the document DB84 could be made available. And this is the ECMM report that we spoke about. I have subsequently discovered that it was received, Your Honours, from the -- what was then the European Community monitoring mission in Zagreb, Croatia, what I think is now known as the European Union Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, this is a document that's in English. You won't be able to read it. But I just want to read out a couple of sections for you. This is the document that Mr. Ackerman read out to you, and it refers to a meeting that took place on the 24th of February of 1992, at which you attended along with Rasula and two other individuals, an HDZ representative and the chief of police. And you stated that there were a number of these meetings and that this meeting may well have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If -- is that -- could the document be moved down so that the bottom of the -- yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last two paragraphs in this document refer to the following. And I'll read it to you. And this is -- it's stated to be exactly from the document. This is local political propaganda which was translated by their interpreter -- by the ECMM interpreter. And it reads as follows. "Serbian people of Sanski Most, you realise the game of Izetbegovic about sovereign and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which he wants to create with this referendum. "He says that he will take care of us, that he will provide us with equality of rights as though Serbs are simple minded people, so they need tutor about that kind of sovereignty. "5.000 Serbs were laying on Susnjar are telling us and who is trying are still being hurt. "Thanks to god there are no more nife Serbs. Otherwise President Izetbegovic would succeed in his aim and we be all living in this Islamic Bosnia. "Every Serb who would participate in this referendum would actually vote for his dependence and would portray his family and his inheritance. "But there are not such Serbs, and President Izetbegovic was wrong if he thought that way because Serbs are sovereign people living on their own territory and they have their own country made by their own will. "Izetbegovic's will is Serbs trouble." And then it has in brackets, "T," which I suspect means translated, "by our interpreter." Now, Mr. Karabeg, this is contained in an ECMM document that's been put to you by the Defence. Do you recall hearing that kind of propaganda in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did hear at the time this type of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you hear this kind of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say. That was the leadership of the SDS through their contacts and visits to the Serbian people, the Serb ethnic groups. And something similar would be also found on flyers with a warning that the Serbian people shouldn't participate at the referendum concerning the issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to read to you the on collusion in this document.
